summary: A first-person narrator in San Francisco notes how quickly 'DON'T TRUST ANYONE OVER 25' merchandise has spread from online memes into shop windows, and recalls a Social Studies class where teacher Ms Galvez writes the slogan on the board. Ms Galvez uses the phrase to introduce the 1960s, tying hippie culture to the civil rights movement and the politics of Berkeley and California. The excerpt is a fragment that breaks off mid-sentence about student activism at Berkeley.
one_line: A San Francisco narrator sees the 'DON'T TRUST ANYONE OVER 25' slogan spread into shop merchandise, then hears a teacher link it to 1960s civil rights and student politics.
key_facts: The narrator planned to get one of the Emma Goldman posters and detoured to 16th and Mission on the way to an unnamed destination.
The store at 16th and Mission was shut, but the narrator read its hours off the door and confirmed the poster was still displayed.
Half the shops in the neighborhood had DON'T TRUST merchandise in their windows, including lunchboxes, babydoll tees, pencil-boxes, and trucker hats.
The narrator says that as new memes spread online, stores have become faster at putting matching merch in their windows.
A jet-pack video made of carbonated water would appear in inboxes on Monday, and by Tuesday t-shirts with stills from it could be bought.
Distressed designer jeans carried the slogan written in what looked like high school ball-point ink.
The slogan 'DON'T TRUST ANYONE OVER 25' was written on the blackboard when the narrator got to Ms Galvez's Social Studies class.
Ms Galvez set down her SchoolBook, powered it up, and turned to face the board with chalk in hand.
Ms Galvez joked that 'Inflation has hit the nation's slogan-writers, it seems' and asked where the phrase came from.
A student guessed 'Hippies?' and Ms Galvez said the phrase is tied to the sixties, when clothes and music were incidental to the era's main political story.
Ms Galvez said California was one of the main places civil rights leaders came from and was more political than the rest of the country.
Black workers in California had access to union factory jobs on the same terms as white workers, so they were better off than their cousins in the South.
The excerpt ends mid-sentence as Ms Galvez begins describing how the students at Berkeley sent a steady stream of activists.
